steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our dataset paper releasing EEG and EMG recordings of people wearing an active orthosis that makes errors. Motivate it from EEG use with exoskeletons and error-related potentials, point out the research gap, describe what the dataset offers, and give an outline of the paper.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:

  - EEG: infer subjective correctness of robot behavior the human observes/interacts with
  - EEG: teach subjective preferences to a prosthesis

- Challenges
  - asynchronous classification needed -> many false positives with long interaction/task times
  - most studies: visual stimuli; only one study uses tactile stimuli to elicit ErrP
  - only rather complex errors shown to elicit ErrP or frequency-domain changes
  - simple, obvious errors not yet studied
- Gap and dataset
  - other modalities than visual should be studied
  - what complexity of task/response/interaction errors elicits ErrP
  - continuous classification; separating overlapping EEG activities
  - lack of open data; robots limit which groups can do this research
  - dataset: 8 subjects, active orthosis introducing simple errors
  - details of active elbow orthosis (simple, replicable); experimental procedure (error complexity, instructions, explicit responses or not)
- Hope
  - first open-access dataset; EEG for more natural, individualized support in activities of daily living; important for rehabilitation
- Structure
  - Section 3: experimental design, methods, data format, folder structure
  - Section 4: preliminary quality analysis (response-time, event-related potential)
  - Section 5: overview, future possibilities

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Exoskeletons and orthoses are often used to assist human movement or make it possible (see <<1|a review>>). They can even augment classical therapy approaches like mirror therapy <<2>>. The electroencephalogram (EEG) can be used to infer the intention to move, and also to trigger the assistance that an exoskeleton gives <<1>>. This has been shown to be very important for successful neuro-rehabilitation <<3,4>>. EEG can also be used to infer the subjective correctness of the behavior of a robot that the human observes or interacts with, as several works have shown <<5,6,7>>. EEG activity can also be used to teach subjective preferences to a prosthesis, as was proposed in earlier work <<8>>. Also, misbehavior of an assistive device can be detected with the error-related potentials (ErrPs) that occur when the brain observes errors <<9>>.

Inferring errors from EEG is hard because it needs asynchronous classification of the relevant patterns in the EEG, and this often gives many false positives because of long interaction times with the system or long task times for the system <<10,11,12,13>>. Most studies look at how the brain evaluates erroneous behavior with visual stimuli, and according to our literature review there is only one study that uses tactile stimuli to elicit an ErrP <<14>>. Also, it has only been shown that rather complex errors in behavior elicit the ErrP or correlated changes in the frequency domain. How the brain responds to simpler errors, which are quite obvious and may not need much evaluation to assess correctness, has not been studied yet.

- Gap: other modalities than visual; what error complexity elicits ErrP; continuous classification; separating partially overlapping EEG activities

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Exoskeletons and orthoses are often used to assist human movement or make it possible (see a review). They can even augment classical therapy approaches like mirror therapy. The electroencephalogram (EEG) can be used to infer the intention to move, and also to trigger the assistance that an exoskeleton gives. This has been shown to be very important for successful neuro-rehabilitation. EEG can also be used to infer the subjective correctness of the behavior of a robot that the human observes or interacts with, as several works have shown. EEG activity can also be used to teach subjective preferences to a prosthesis, as was proposed in earlier work. Also, misbehavior of an assistive device can be detected with the error-related potentials (ErrPs) that occur when the brain observes errors.

Inferring errors from EEG is hard because it needs asynchronous classification of the relevant patterns in the EEG, and this often gives many false positives because of long interaction times with the system or long task times for the system. Most studies look at how the brain evaluates erroneous behavior with visual stimuli, and according to our literature review there is only one study that uses tactile stimuli to elicit an ErrP. Also, it has only been shown that rather complex errors in behavior elicit the ErrP or correlated changes in the frequency domain. How the brain responds to simpler errors, which are quite obvious and may not need much evaluation to assess correctness, has not been studied yet.

Based on the literature we think there is a gap in the research on error-related activity. Other modalities than the visual modality should be studied more closely, during the interaction or as a source of feedback, in terms of what activities they cause in the brain. We also need to understand better what complexity in task, response, or interaction errors is needed to elicit the ErrP. Methods for continuous classification of error-related activity, and methods that can distinguish between different, partially overlapping EEG activities, should also be explored more. Here there is a particular lack of openly accessible data that would let a larger research community contribute. Also, using robots limits the number of research groups that can do research on these problems. For this reason we recorded a dataset of 8 subjects wearing an active orthosis device that introduces simple errors into its behavior. We also give details about the active elbow orthosis, since it is a fairly simple robotic system that could let other groups replicate the work or extend it. The experimental procedure is described too, which gives relevant information about the error complexity, the subject instructions, and whether subjects should respond explicitly to errors or not.

We hope this first open-access dataset will enable broader research on how assistive technology can be improved by using EEG to give more natural and individualized support for activities of daily living. This kind of support is very important for rehabilitation.

The rest of the paper is structured like this. Section 3 gives detailed information about the experimental design and the methods used to record the dataset, and also describes the data format and folder structure so the dataset is easier to understand. Section 4 presents a preliminary quality analysis of the recorded data, in the form of a response-time analysis and an event-related potential analysis. Finally, Section 5 gives an overview of the experiment and discusses future possibilities.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Exoskeletons and orthoses are frequently used to assist or enable human movement (see [1]). They can even augment classical therapy approaches such as mirror therapy [2]. The electroencephalogram (EEG) can be used not only to infer the intention to move but also to trigger the assistance provided by an exoskeleton [1], which has been shown to be very important for successful neuro-rehabilitation [3,4]. It can also be used to infer the subjective correctness of the behavior of a robot that the human observes or interacts with, as shown in several works such as [5,6,7]. EEG activity can also enable the teaching of subjective preferences to a prosthesis, as proposed by [8]. Furthermore, misbehavior of an assistive device can be detected using the error-related potentials (ErrPs) that occur when the brain observes errors [9].

Inferring errors from EEG is challenging because it requires asynchronous classification of relevant patterns in the EEG, which often leads to many false positives due to long interaction times with the system or long task times for the system [10,11,12,13]. While most studies focus on how the brain evaluates erroneous behavior using visual stimuli, according to our literature review only one study uses tactile stimuli to elicit an ErrP [14]. Moreover, it has only been shown that rather complex errors in behavior elicit the ErrP or correlated changes in the frequency domain. How the brain responds to simpler errors that are quite obvious and may not require extensive evaluation to assess correctness has not yet been studied.

Based on the available literature, we believe there is a gap in the research on error-related activity. Modalities other than the visual modality should be studied more closely during the interaction or as a source of feedback, in terms of what activities they induce in the brain. It is also necessary to better understand what complexity in task, response, or interaction errors is required to elicit the ErrP. Furthermore, methods for continuous classification of error-related activity and methods that can distinguish between different, partially overlapping EEG activities should be explored more intensively. In this regard, there is a particular lack of openly accessible data that would allow a larger research community to contribute, and the use of robots limits the number of research groups that can conduct research on such problems. For this reason, we recorded a dataset of 8 subjects wearing an active orthosis device that introduces simple errors in its behavior. We also provide details about the active elbow orthosis, as it is a fairly simple robotic system that could allow other groups to replicate or extend the work. The experimental procedure is described as well, giving relevant information about the error complexity, subject instructions, and whether or not subjects should respond explicitly to errors.

We hope that this first open-access dataset will enable broader research on how assistive technology can be improved by using EEG to provide more natural and individualized support for activities of daily living. Such support is very important for rehabilitation [15].

The rest of the paper is structured as follows. Section 3 provides detailed information about the experimental design and the methods used to record the dataset, and describes the data format and folder structure for a better understanding of the dataset. Section 4 presents a preliminary quality analysis of the recorded data in the form of response-time analysis and event-related potential analysis. Finally, Section 5 provides an overview of this experiment and discusses future possibilities.
